items.headline: 穆里尼奧紀錄片、新書書評
items.context: Netflix 推出足球教練穆里尼奧（José Mourinho）的三集紀錄片，由曾拍過《Bros: After the Screaming Stops》的導演喬・波爾曼（Joe Pearlman）執導；劇評形容穆里尼奧全片顯得防備心重，片尾他自己也說「你在逼我談自己……而我不想。」書市方面，記者瑞秋・阿維夫（Rachel Aviv）推出新書《You Won't Get Free of It》，收錄六篇原刊於《紐約客》、探討母女關係的紀實故事，其中一篇寫到心理學家伊莉莎白・洛夫特斯（Elizabeth Loftus）——她曾為包括哈維・溫斯坦（Harvey Weinstein）在內的多起訴訟擔任專家證人。

sources.summary: Football manager José Mourinho stars in a three-parter from the creators of Bros: After the Screaming Stops. Don’t expect it to be quite so entertaining… Among his previous credits, the director of this mini-series Joe Pearlman can count the revelatory and hilarious 2018 film, Bros: After the Screaming Stops . That documentary worked brilliantly because its subjects seemed so sweetly but devastatingly lacking in discretion or self-awareness that everything they said landed like a line from a Christopher Guest parody. They couldn’t help themselves. In terms of a character study, storied football manager José Mourinho is a very different kettle of cold fish. Like the Goss twins, he takes himself very seriously indeed, but that’s pretty much where the similarities end. He’s something of a closed book. “You are pushing me to speak about myself,” he says, towards the end of the final part of this series. “And I don’t want to.” Which is fair enough but it does beg the question: why then, would you agree to be the subject of an in-depth three part documentary series? sources.summary: The most complex of female relationships is thrown into sharp relief in this moving series of essays Rachel Aviv has a profound interest in the vagaries of human psychology: Strangers to Ourselves, her last book, profiled five people whose psychiatric states resisted straightforward explanation, testing the limits of the mental health system. A Pulitzer finalist, Aviv has become known for rigorous, penetrating journalism that is as empathic as it is insightful. Now comes You Won’t Get Free of It, six stories of mothers and daughters, all originally published in the New Yorker. Madness runs through this book, too, in the stories of Linda Bishop, a woman who, upon discharge from hospital after a psychotic break, holed up in an abandoned farmhouse and tried to subsist on apples alone, and of Mary, a woman whose delusions and paranoia were only seemingly cured as a side-effect of chemotherapy. It’s also there in the childhood memories of the psychologist Elizabeth Loftus – a professional court witness for those who have been accused of abuse, one of whom was Harvey Weinstein. Loftus’s mother was found drowned, perhaps as a result of suicide. In Aviv’s masterly profile, she teases out a conclusion that leaves you pondering the extent to which this memory expert can rely on her own recollections, and what that says about her particular line of work. sources.summary: Offerman leads a talented cast, but this preschool picture book spinoff fails to inspire Grumpy Mr Fish (Nick Offerman) has a reputation for being a sourpuss, but when he teams up with baby sea dragon Pip (Nina Oyama) to locate a wish-granting fish, it’s pretty much guaranteed that we will discover some sort of heart of gold lurking beneath his gloomy exterior. Not that a picture book for the two to four-year-old crowd can’t be expanded into a satisfying narrative feature film universe, but this high seas adventure as personal growth is fairly by-the-numbers stuff. Based on the books by Deborah Diesen and Dan Hanna, The Pout-Pout Fish’s animation lacks the charm of the books’ illustrations, and the writing is uninspired. Sample exposition-dump: “Did you not hear what they just said? Someone else is looking for Shimmer! And they’ve got a head start! If they get to her first, she won’t have any wish power left!” When the script tries to be more distinctive, you kind of wish they hadn’t bothered – a trio of pink dolphins reference lip-fillers and parody Mean Girls in a way that will be utterly meaningless to the tots at whom the film is aimed, while not being clever enough for their parents. Even the fact that the dolphins are voiced by Amy Sedaris doesn’t help much. So is there anything to like ? The lead character’s vocal stylings are a high point, because Offerman does have one of the great voices. (His entertaining autobiography Paddle Your Own Canoe is well worth the audiobook version.) The man’s voice – an exquisite walnut burr, burnished to a deep amber lustre – can almost, though not quite, elevate bland fare like this uninspiring effort. It’s pretty much the only reason to watch, or at the very least, listen. Continue reading...

sources.summary: Summerhall, Edinburgh Gregory Nussen spins Italo Calvino’s surrealist authorial intrusions into a fascinating, playful and political show How to adapt an unadaptable novel famed for its postmodern surrealism and authorial intrusions? For Los Angeles performer Gregory Nussen, there can be only one solution: a play built out of postmodern surrealism and authorial intrusions. That is what becomes of Italo Calvino’s If on a Winter’s Night a Traveller as filtered, refracted and reinvented by Nussen and directed by Hannah Pilkes. What in 1979 was a head-spinning novel about the reader trying to make sense of the novel’s unrelated manuscripts becomes, with the actor’s charm, wit and storytelling chops, a playful one-person show that has a fierce political heart beneath its metatheatrical games. sources.summary: This new adaptation of Michael Ende’s 1973 novel contains some neat parables for our digitally nihilistic age, but even a mystical tortoise can’t save it it from monotony Momo – the 1973 fantasy novel by German author Michael Ende, who also wrote The Neverending Story – has been adapted in live and animated forms before, in 1986 and 2001. This latest version, too, is ostensibly a live-action film – but it’s been made with so many visual effects it might as well have been a cartoon. Still, the residual human element represented by the cast feels necessary, given the story is about the dangers of letting capitalism suck away our ability to enjoy the moment. Over the years, readers have posited all kinds of metaphorical interpretations of the plot, which involves a world where grey beings arrive and con everyone into literally “banking” their time, so as to have it all to themselves. Only the urchin Momo, here played by teen actor Alexa Goodall (whose gorgeous supernova of ginger curls is practically another character in the film), can save the world. Continue reading...

sources.summary: Traverse theatre, Edinburgh A grandmother welcomes her family to a birthday bash in a muddled play that addresses its key theme too late A celebratory family get-together leads to an almighty conflagration in Morna Young’s play. The birthday party reunion is a well-worn storytelling trope for explosive family reckonings – the Traverse featured another such party this time last year with Consumed, directed by Katie Posner , who helms this production, too. Co-created by Young and Alex Fthenakis, the twist here is that flamboyant matriarch Vivienne (Alison Peebles), known as “glam-ma” to her grandchildren, is throwing an 80th birthday party and then plans to die the very next day. She has terminal cancer so has arranged her death, although we are not told how she has managed that, given assisted dying is currently illegal in Scotland , as well as England and Wales. Is this a near or alternate future – or merely wishful thinking? Continue reading...

sources.name: The Guardian
sources.summary: Two likely lads in their 20s deal with problematic lives that dramatically intersect in this persuasive London drama This gritty crime drama unfolds entirely within the Punjabi community in London’s Hounslow district, a plausible demographic situation in which white people are so peripheral to the story that they are little more than extras. In fact watching this well-crafted, if somewhat melodramatic, debut for director Jazz Bhalla makes one wonder why there aren’t more films made in the UK with entirely British Asian casts. Here, it doesn’t makes the film better or worse, but it certainly feels realistic and true to its milieu. The story revolves around two best friends in their 20s, Ravi (Amar Chaggar) and Jay (Jayant Singh), likely lads who spend a lot of time hanging out, getting high or drunk and ending nearly every sentence with the word “bro”. On the face of it, Jay seems like the one with a more stable situation at home, living with his middle-class parents; while Ravi, who has a criminal record due to a drug bust, lives in a bedsit and is estranged from his mother ever since his father died and she remarried, much to the chagrin of his bossy older sister (Parvinder Shergill). But Ravi manages to get a job working for a building supply merchant, which compels him to start waking up at dawn and considering the downside of always being hung over. sources.summary: Pleasance Courtyard, Edinburgh With the air of a hungover postmortem, Richardson gives a head-spinning account of an encounter with an older comedian If you’re partial to a bit of gossip and scandal, Harriet Richardson is your girl. In this gloriously juicy debut hour, she dishes the dirt on the DMs she received from an older comedian and the intense, utterly absorbing events that followed. Yes, she found his eBay account. And yes, she spent six months tracking him down on a dating app only to play his profile song hundreds of times. But what else is a girl driven by obsession supposed to do? We meet Richardson, who until now has worked primarily as a performance artist, all smiles and ready to share. She takes us back to the creation of her 2024 viral piece 100 Dates , in which she spent Valentine’s Day online speed-dating in an attempt to analyse her relationship with infatuation and connection. The comedian in question used the project as the opening line of his first message to her. What followed is flirtation so blatant it makes your toes curl: “Do you want to see my trophy?”; a string of saucy snaps; and finally a frantic voice note from the comedian’s manager bringing the whole messaging saga to an abrupt end. sources.summary: Gilded Balloon Teviot, Edinburgh Performer cleared of death of her roommate in Italy uses new motherhood as framework for her defiant comedy show ‘Welcome to the most controversial show on the fringe !” Some audiences will diagnose self-regard in that intro by rookie standup Amanda Knox. For others, as for Knox herself, it merely acknowledges the continuing efforts to silence her. But then, Knox is “the human version of the blue/gold dress”, a canvas on to which we all project guilty, innocent – or weird. Her innocence now proved, it’s the last of these charges she takes on in this fringe outing, retelling her oft-told tale through the lens of new motherhood. Is it a disgrace that she’s telling it at all – and profiting from it, some would say (although they’ve presumably never taken a show to the Edinburgh fringe)? Classifying Cartwheel as comedy may be a misstep; it risks looking insensitive and inaccurately describes the show. But, judging by the evidence, Knox would be damned whatever she did. Now at least she can tell her story in her own way, articulating a growing anger at her treatment and a determination to raise her daughter, not to be silenced and scared but “to be the exact girl I was punished for being”. items.headline: 重要人員赴中禁攜公務機
items.context: 數位發展部資通安全署11日公布『公務出國資通訊設備管理須知』，目的是防範公務人員出國執行公務時的資料外洩風險。其中，涉及國安或重大利益、被歸類為『重要人員』者，若因公前往中國、香港、澳門等高資安風險地區，將不得攜帶平常使用的公務資通訊裝備，返國後臨時配發的設備也須進行資安檢測。

items.voice_text: 公務員出國，以後不能亂帶公務手機了。數位發展部資通安全署，公布了一份新規定，叫做『公務出國資通訊設備管理須知』，目的是防範公務人員出國時的資料外洩風險。其中，被歸類為『重要人員』——也就是涉及國安或重大利益的人——如果因公前往中國、香港、澳門這些高資安風險地區，就不能帶平常用的公務資通訊裝備。返國之後，臨時配發的設備，也要做資安檢測。
